title: What compliance training must Medicare Advantage and Part D sponsors provide?
description: Medicare Advantage and Part D compliance training under 42 CFR 422.503 and 423.504: annual, at orientation, board included, as at November 2026.
shortAnswer: The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) requires Medicare Advantage organizations and Part D plan sponsors to provide effective compliance training and education to the compliance officer, employees, the chief executive, senior administrators, managers and governing body members. Under 42 CFR 422.503(b)(4)(vi)(C) and 423.504(b)(4)(vi)(C), training must occur at a minimum annually and be part of orientation for new employees and new appointments to chief executive, manager or governing body roles.
keyTakeaways: Effective training and education is one of the seven core elements of the compliance program that every Medicare Advantage (Part C) organization and Part D sponsor must adopt.
The regulation names the audience: the compliance officer, employees, the chief executive and other senior administrators, managers, and governing body members.
Timing: at a minimum annually, and as part of orientation for new employees and for anyone newly appointed as chief executive, manager, or governing body member.

CMS's Compliance Program Guidelines (Medicare Managed Care Manual chapter 21 and Prescription Drug Benefit Manual chapter 9) add detail, such as training within 90 days of hire and proof of completion.

A 2018 final rule removed the CMS requirement for first tier, downstream and related entities (FDRs) to complete compliance and fraud, waste and abuse training. Older guidance that describes FDR training predates that change.
regulator: Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS), US Department of Health and Human Services
appliesTo: Medicare Advantage (MA) organizations under 42 CFR Part 422
Medicare Part D plan sponsors under 42 CFR Part 423
Their compliance officers, employees, chief executives, senior administrators, managers and governing body members

sections.heading: Who must provide Medicare compliance program training?

blocks.text: Medicare Advantage organizations and Part D plan sponsors must provide it, as a condition of their contracts with CMS. The requirement is part of the administrative and management arrangements in [42 CFR 422.503(b)(4)(vi)](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/42/422.503) for MA organizations and [42 CFR 423.504(b)(4)(vi)](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/42/423.504) for Part D sponsors. Both require the sponsor to "adopt and implement an effective compliance program" with measures that prevent, detect, and correct non-compliance with CMS program requirements and fraud, waste, and abuse.

For readers outside the United States: Medicare is the US federal health insurance program. Part C (Medicare Advantage) and Part D (prescription drug coverage) are delivered by private organizations under contract with CMS, which is why CMS sets compliance program rules for those organizations. This page cites the Cornell Legal Information Institute mirror of the CFR and states the position as at November 2026.
The regulation requires effective training and education for a named audience, at least annually and at orientation. The MA text reads:

blocks.title: 42 CFR 422.503(b)(4)(vi)(C)
blocks.text: "(1) Each MA organization must establish and implement effective training and education for its compliance officer and organization employees, the MA organization's chief executive and other senior administrators, managers and governing body members. (2) Such training and education must occur at a minimum annually and must be made a part of the orientation for a new employee and new appointment to a chief executive, manager, or governing body member."

The Part D text in 423.504(b)(4)(vi)(C) is the same in substance, with "Part D plan sponsor" in place of "MA organization." The 2018 rule discussed below aligned the two paragraphs deliberately, to remove any ambiguity about timing. Neither paragraph sets hours, a curriculum, or a delivery format.

sections.heading: How does training fit into the seven compliance program elements?

blocks.text: Training is element (C) of seven core requirements, and it supports most of the others. Each element in 422.503(b)(4)(vi) and 423.504(b)(4)(vi) creates something staff must know about.

blocks.caption: The seven core compliance program requirements and what training must convey
head: Element
Requirement (summary)
What training must convey
rows: Written policies, procedures and standards of conduct, including non-intimidation and non-retaliation
The standards of conduct, how to raise compliance issues, and protection for good faith reporting.
Compliance officer and compliance committee; governing body knowledgeable about the program
Who the compliance officer is, and for the board, the content and operation of the program.
Effective training and education
The training element itself.
Effective, confidential lines of communication, including anonymous good faith reporting
How and where to report, including anonymously.
Well-publicized disciplinary standards
Expectations for reporting and the consequences of non-compliance.
Routine monitoring and identification of compliance risks
That monitoring and audits occur and how staff take part.
Prompt response to compliance issues and corrective action
How issues are investigated and corrected, including retraining.

blocks.text: Element (B)(3) is particularly relevant to board education: "The governing body of the MA organization must be knowledgeable about the content and operation of the compliance program and must exercise reasonable oversight with respect to the implementation and effectiveness of the compliance programs." Governing body training is therefore both a training requirement and the evidence for an oversight requirement. See [how to report training compliance to the board](/guides/how-to-report-training-compliance-to-the-board).

sections.heading: What does CMS guidance add about timing, content and proof?

blocks.text: CMS's [Compliance Program Guidelines](https://www.cms.gov/Regulations-and-Guidance/Guidance/Manuals/Downloads/mc86c21.pdf), published as Medicare Managed Care Manual chapter 21 and Prescription Drug Benefit Manual chapter 9, add operational detail. Section 50.3.1 states that employees (including temporary workers and volunteers) and governing body members "must, at a minimum, receive general compliance training within 90 days of initial hiring, and annually thereafter."

items: **Delivery:** examples include classroom training, online modules, or attestations that employees have read the standards of conduct and compliance policies.
**Proof:** sponsors "must be able to demonstrate" completion, for example with sign-in sheets, employee attestations, and electronic certifications.
**Review:** sponsors should review and update general compliance training when there are material changes in regulations, policy or guidance, and at least annually.

**Topics:** examples include the compliance program and standards of conduct, how to ask questions and report noncompliance, non-retaliation, disciplinary guidelines, conflicts of interest, HIPAA and confidentiality, and the laws that govern employee conduct in the Medicare program.

**Fraud, waste and abuse (FWA):** section 50.3.2 describes FWA training within 90 days of hire and annually, covering laws such as the False Claims Act and the Anti-Kickback Statute, reporting processes, and whistleblower protections.

blocks.title: Check the date of the guidance
blocks.text: The chapter is dated January 2013 (chapter 21 Rev. 110; chapter 9 Rev. 16). Its descriptions of training for first tier, downstream and related entities predate the 2018 regulatory change described below, so those passages should not be read as current CMS requirements without checking.

sections.heading: Do first tier, downstream and related entities still need CMS training?

blocks.text: Not as a CMS requirement. In the [Contract Year 2019 final rule](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2018/04/16/2018-07179/medicare-program-contract-year-2019-policy-and-technical-changes-to-the-medicare-advantage-medicare), published on April 16, 2018, CMS stated: "This provision eliminates Parts C and D compliance program and FWA training for FDRs." CMS finalized the proposal without modification, and the current regulation text names only the sponsor's own compliance officer, employees, senior leaders, managers and governing body.

CMS also said that FDRs remain required to comply with all statutes, regulations and program requirements, that sponsors remain accountable for their FDRs, and that sponsors may continue to impose training requirements through their contracts. A sponsor that wants FDR staff trained must therefore require it through the contract as part of FDR oversight, rather than relying on a CMS mandate.

sections.heading: How can sponsors map the requirement to outcomes and evidence?

blocks.text: Map each audience and trigger in the regulation to an outcome and the evidence an auditor will request. The mapping below is illustrative.

head: Requirement
Example learning outcome
Evidence to retain
rows: (C)(2) Orientation, new employee
Explains the standards of conduct and how to report suspected noncompliance or FWA.
Completion within the sponsor's defined onboarding window (CMS guidance: 90 days), with content version.
(C)(2) Annual training
Applies current policies to job-specific compliance scenarios.
Annual completion records for all employees, temporary workers and volunteers.
(C)(1) Governing body
Describes the content and operation of the compliance program and the board's oversight role.
Board training records, agendas, and compliance officer reports received.
(C)(2) New appointment
A new chief executive or manager explains their compliance responsibilities.
Orientation record dated from the appointment.
(E) and (G) Retraining

blocks.text: For the general method, see [how to map training to compliance obligations](/guides/how-to-map-training-to-compliance-obligations). For the US Department of Justice's view of compliance training in any corporate compliance program, see [DOJ compliance program training expectations](/regulations/doj-compliance-program-training-expectations).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry maps each of the seven compliance program elements to the sponsor's own policies, the roles that must be trained (including governing body members), and the assessment points that evidence understanding. When a policy or CMS requirement changes, the affected content and audiences can be identified from those links. See how this works for [healthcare and life sciences organizations](/industries/healthcare-life-sciences).

faqs.q: How soon must new employees complete Medicare compliance training?
faqs.a: The regulation says training must be part of orientation for new employees. CMS's Compliance Program Guidelines (section 50.3.1) set a practical benchmark: general compliance training within 90 days of initial hiring and annually thereafter. Sponsors should document their own onboarding window and apply it consistently.

faqs.q: Do board members have to complete compliance training?
faqs.a: Yes. Governing body members are named in 422.503(b)(4)(vi)(C)(1) and 423.504(b)(4)(vi)(C)(1), and new governing body appointments must receive training as part of orientation. Separately, the governing body must be knowledgeable about the content and operation of the compliance program and exercise reasonable oversight.

faqs.q: Can attestations count as compliance training?
faqs.a: CMS's guidelines list attestations that employees have read and received the standards of conduct or compliance policies as one example of how sponsors may satisfy general compliance training. The regulation still requires training to be effective, so attestation alone may be hard to defend for complex roles.

faqs.q: How long should training records be kept?
faqs.a: Section 50.3.2 of CMS's guidelines states that sponsors are accountable for maintaining FWA training records, including time, attendance, topic, certificates and test scores, for 10 years. Sponsors should confirm current record retention expectations against their CMS contract and the applicable regulations.
